title: A New Orleans band in Dallas and Price on piano in the wrong key
summary: He fills in for the homesick pianist Octave with Sherman Cook's New Orleans band and struggles with an out-of-tune piano, then pulls a gun.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: I'd heard of him, yeah, because see, back when I was coming through that period of Charleston and all that, there was a New Orleans band that came from New Orleans with Professor Sherman Cook. Professor Sherman Cook, Lee Collins, a little boy named LeRoy...I can't think of LeRoy's last name. Percy Darensbourg, Caffrey Darensbourg, Freddie Bobo and a fellow named Octave playing the piano.

I'll tell you about this band from New Orleans. I could only play 'My Isle of Golden Dreams,' or a few songs, or if you start a song off, you know, I could probably come in. So this band--Son Lewis and Cal Liston, who had a dance hall they called it the Skunk...well, they called it...what the hell, some dance hall in Dallas. And they used to like go to other towns and have dances two or three days a week.

So then they said...they needed a piano player. And the piano player, Octave, got high and got homesick for some of that gum-bo and, you know, just...You know, and those fellows couldn't contain themselves. They just went like insane, you know, not to do anything harmful, but just longing for home, you know? So this guy went home. And they said, "Well, we've got to have a piano player to play the dance," so they picked me. And I said to them, "Now look, I'm no piano player when it come down to this business. But if you start a song off, you know like if we're playing 'Sheik' and you stomp it off, da-da-da, when you play the first few notes then I can come in. But don't depend on me to come in and leading it."

That was agreeable, Dan. And then when we got to Mineral Wells, or Wichita Falls or wherever the hell it was, everything changed. They'd bring the music; "Now, in the fourteenth bar you will do this and do that." Now we discover that the piano is not in tune. So in order for them to play in B-flat, I would have to play in B-natural. Well, I couldn't play in B-flat too well to begin with. Now, if they're puttin' me in B-natural, I'm really in trouble. So, this night these guys start a song. I couldn't come in because I'd have to play in B-natural. If I played the chords, if I knew them, I'd be playing in the wrong key.
So they did that to me for two or three days. And I told them, "Now," you know what I mean, "Let's cool it." But what they would always do, Dan, and I guess this is typical of any

person that..where there are two or three people can speak a different language from one person, they'll speak in that language and say something and even if they're not talking about the person, he will think they're talking about him. They used to speak this patois, so coming back from Mineral Wells or wherever it was--we were in this big Cadillac, we had all the instruments and all this business--and they kept talking that patois and I was in the back and I came out with a gun and fired and you're talking about Frenchmen leaving--you ever see rats leave a ship--I ran 'em all down the highway and wouldn't let them come back to the car, and the guy that was the manager, they were coming in a car behind us and they saw all these Frenchmen all around.."b'uhbluhbluhbluhbluh," you know, it killed me (laughter). So finally, Cal Liston say, "Put that gun away," you know what I mean. So I got in the car with the manager and then I went back to Dallas. They never forgot that incident out on the highway, but...because... and the guy drivin' the car, we called him Trembling Slim. He said, "I told you all don't mess with Sam Price, that's one of the Price Boys." (Laughter).
